newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cohen gives pep talk to U.S. troops in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Cohen gives pep talk to U.S. troops in Japan.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, worried that sex scandals have hurt the image of U.S. forces in Japan, gave the troops a pep talk on Tuesday, telling them they were their nation's ambassadors.
In speeches at two major U.S. bases near Tokyo, Cohen paid tribute to the troops' role in maintaining stability in Asia but warned them not to let their guard down off duty.
Troop behaviour in Japan has come under close scrutiny since September 1995, when three servicemen raped an Okinawan schoolgirl, setting off a campaign to shut U.S. bases in Japan.

The issue flared again the week before Cohen arrived when a sailor at one of the bases he visited, the U.S. Navy's headquarters at Yokosuka, was placed in custody on suspicion of beating and sexually assaulting his Japanese girlfriend.
"Remember, you are in effect an ambassador of the United States," Cohen said in a breakfast meeting with airmen and airwomen at Yokota Air Base on the outskirts of Tokyo.

"Every one of you understand, and everyone understands, that you can do 100 good deeds and you will get credit for it," he said. "On the other hand, one bad deed, and that makes the headline news and changes people's perception of what we are doing as a nation.
"So I hope that you will keep that in mind as we pay great respect to you," he added.

Cohen, brought in by President Bill Clinton with a brief to raise the moral image of the military, later took the same message to sailors at Yokosuka naval base, 35 miles (55 km) southeast of the capital.
Japanese police, who have taken over the case of the sailor at Yokosuka, have since ruled out sexual assault and are treating the matter as a case of domestic violence.
Cohen told sailors on board the U.S. missile cruiser Bunker Hill that "you are deeply appreciated by everyone in the United States".
But, he cautioned again: "Every time you step off this ship you are our ambassadors of goodwill."
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has as much interest as Cohen in ensuring a better image for U.S. troops.
Each time there is an incident, groups opposed to the U.S. military presence seize on it as a reason why they should leave Japan.

On Sunday, several thousand people held a protest rally in Tokyo against the presence of the forces on Okinawa, an island which makes up less than one percent of Japan's land area but hosts the bulk of U.S. military facilities in Japan.
In a non-binding referendum last year, Okinawans backed a drive by the island's governor to have all the bases closed by 2015.
The concentration of U.S. military facilities on Okinawa is a legacy of the U.S. military occupation of the island from 1945 until 1972, when it was returned to Japan.

Since arriving in Tokyo on Monday, Cohen has heard pledges from Hashimoto, as well as his Defence Agency chief Fumio Kyuma, that Japan does not seek a cutback in the present level of 100,000 U.S. military personnel in Asia, including 47,000 in Japan.
Cohen said he planned to assure Hashimoto in a meeting on Wednesday of Washington's determination to also keep 100,000 American military personnel in the western Pacific indefinitely.
"At the cornerstone of our relationship as a Pacific power lies the country of Japan," Cohen told the sailors on the Bunker Hill.
